paragraphs: “Those cultivated parents put this poor five-year-old through every torture imaginable. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason, until her whole body was one bruise. Then they got more refined in their cruelty. They locked her up all night in an outhouse, in the cold and frost. And because she hadn’t asked to be taken out in the night (as if a five-year-old, sleeping her sound, angelic sleep, could be trained to wake and ask!), they smeared her face with excrement and filled her mouth with it, and it was her mother, her own mother, who did this. And that mother could sleep while she heard the poor child groaning! Can you understand why a little creature, who can’t even grasp what is being done to her, should beat her aching little heart with her tiny fist in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, unresentful tears to ‘dear, kind God’ to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend and brother, you pious, humble novice? Do you understand why this infamy has to exist and is allowed to? I’m told that without it man couldn’t have lived on earth, since he wouldn’t have known good and evil. Why should he know that diabolical good and evil, when it costs so much? The whole world of knowledge isn’t worth that child’s prayer to ‘dear, kind God’! I say nothing about the suffering of grown-up people. They ate the apple, damn them, and the devil take them all! But these little ones! I’m making you suffer, Alyosha. You’re not yourself. I’ll stop if you like.”
“Never mind. I want to suffer too,” muttered Alyosha.

“One more picture, just one, because it’s so curious and so typical. I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities, and I’ve forgotten the name. I’ll have to look it up. It happened in the darkest days of serfdom, early in the century, and long live the Liberator of the People! In those days there was a general with aristocratic connections who owned great estates. He was one of those men (somewhat exceptional even then, I believe) who retire from the service into a life of leisure, convinced that it has earned them absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were such men then. So this general settled on his estate of two thousand souls and lived in grand style, lording it over his poor neighbors as if they were hangers-on and jesters. He had kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys, all in uniform and all mounted. One day a serf-boy, a little child of eight, threw a stone in play and hurt the paw of the general’s favorite hound. ‘Why is my favorite dog lame?’ He is told that the boy threw a stone and hurt its paw. ‘So you did it.’ The general looked the child up and down. ‘Take him.’ They took him. They took him from his mother and kept him locked up all night. Early the next morning the general rides out in full hunting parade, with his hounds, his dependents, dog-boys and huntsmen, all mounted around him. The servants are summoned to be edified, and in front of them all stands the child’s mother. The child is brought out of the lock-up. It’s a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day, a capital day for hunting. The general orders the child undressed. The boy is stripped naked. He shivers, numb with terror, not daring to cry.... ‘Make him run,’ commands the general. ‘Run! Run!’ shout the dog-boys. The boy runs.... ‘At him!’ yells the general, and he looses the whole pack on the child. The hounds seize him and tear him to pieces before his mother’s eyes!... I believe the general was later declared unfit to run his estates. Well, what did he deserve? To be shot? To be shot, to satisfy our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!”
“To be shot,” Alyosha murmured, looking up at Ivan with a pale, crooked smile.
“Bravo!” cried Ivan, delighted. “If even you say so.... Some monk you are! So there’s a little devil sitting in your heart, Alyosha Karamazov!”
“What I said was absurd, but—”

“That’s exactly it, that ‘but’!” cried Ivan. “I’ll tell you something, novice: the absurd is only too necessary on earth. The world stands on absurdities, and maybe nothing at all would have happened in it without them. We know what we know!”
“What do you know?”

“I understand nothing,” Ivan went on, as if in delirium. “I don’t want to understand anything now. I want to stay with the fact. I decided long ago not to understand. If I start trying to understand something, I’ll betray the fact, and I’m determined to stay with the fact.”
“Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried, in sudden distress. “Are you going to tell me what you mean, at last?”
“Of course I am. That’s what I’ve been working up to. You’re dear to me. I don’t want to let you go, and I won’t give you up to your Zossima.”
Ivan was silent for a minute, and all at once his face turned very sad.

“Listen! I took up the case of children only to make my point clearer. As for the other tears of humanity, which soak the earth from its crust to its core, I’ll say nothing about them. I’ve narrowed my subject on purpose. I’m a bug, and I admit in all humility that I can’t understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame themselves, I suppose. They were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, knowing they would be made unhappy. So there’s no need to pity them. All I know, with my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian mind, is that there is suffering and nobody is guilty; that cause follows effect plainly and directly; that everything flows and finds its level. But that’s only Euclidian nonsense, I know it, and I can’t agree to live by it! What comfort is it to me that nobody is guilty, that cause follows effect plainly and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I’ll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and place, but here on earth, where I can see it myself. I have believed in it. I want to see it, and if I’m dead by then, let me rise again. If it all happens without me, that will be too unfair. Surely I didn’t suffer just so that my crimes and my sufferings could manure the ground for somebody else’s future harmony. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. Every religion in the world is built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I to do about them? That’s the question I can’t answer. For the hundredth time I say it: there are masses of questions, but I’ve taken only the children, because in their case what I mean is unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer in order to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it? Tell me, please. It’s beyond all understanding why they should suffer, and why they should have to pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, be material to enrich the soil for somebody’s future harmony? I understand solidarity among men in sin. I understand solidarity in retribution, too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it’s really true that they share the responsibility for all their fathers’ crimes, then that truth does not belong to this world, and I can’t comprehend it. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned. But he didn’t grow up, you see. He was torn to pieces by dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I’m not blaspheming! I do understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will have been reached and everything will be clear. But this is exactly where I stop: I can’t accept that harmony. And while I’m still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too, perhaps, may cry out with the rest, as I watch the mother embrace her child’s torturer, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry it out then. While there’s still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It isn’t worth the tears of that one tortured child, who beat her little chest with her little fist and prayed in her stinking outhouse, with her unatoned tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn’t worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How will you atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don’t want any more suffering. And if the suffering of children goes to make up the sum of suffering needed to pay for the truth, then I protest that the truth isn’t worth such a price. I don’t want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to. Let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her own mother’s heart. But the suffering of her tortured child she has no right to forgive. She must not forgive the torturer, even if the child forgave him! And if that’s so, if they have no right to forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could? I don’t want harmony. Out of love for humanity I don’t want it. I’d rather keep my unavenged suffering. I’d rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, _even if I were wrong_. Besides, the price of harmony is too high. It’s beyond our means to pay so much to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I’m an honest man, I’m bound to hand it back as soon as I can. That’s what I’m doing. It isn’t God I don’t accept, Alyosha. I just most respectfully return Him the ticket.”
“That’s rebellion,” murmured Alyosha, looking down.

“Rebellion? I’m sorry you call it that,” said Ivan earnestly. “One can hardly live in rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I challenge you, answer. Suppose you were building the fabric of human destiny, with the aim of making people happy in the end and giving them peace and rest at last. But suppose it was essential and unavoidable to torture to death just one tiny creature, that baby beating her chest with her fist, for example, and to build that edifice on her unavenged tears. Would you agree to be the architect on those terms? Tell me, and tell the truth.”
“No, I wouldn’t agree,” said Alyosha softly.

“And can you accept that the people you were building it for would consent to take their happiness on the foundation of a little victim’s unatoned blood? And that, having taken it, they would stay happy for ever?”

“No, I can’t accept that. Brother,” said Alyosha suddenly, his eyes flashing, “you just asked whether there is a being in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could. But there is a Being, and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and for everything. You’ve forgotten Him, and the edifice is built on Him, and it is to Him they cry aloud, ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed!’”

“Ah! The One without sin, and His blood! No, I haven’t forgotten Him. On the contrary, I’ve been wondering the whole time why you hadn’t brought Him in sooner, since in arguments on your side He usually comes first. Do you know, Alyosha, and don’t laugh, I composed a poem about a year ago. If you can waste another ten minutes on me, I’ll tell it to you.”
“You wrote a poem?”

“Oh, no, I didn’t write it,” laughed Ivan. “I’ve never written two lines of verse in my life. But I made up this poem, in prose, and I remembered it. I got carried away when I made it up. You’ll be my first reader, or rather listener. Why should an author give up even one listener?” smiled Ivan. “Shall I tell it to you?”
“I’m listening,” said Alyosha.
“The poem’s title is ‘The Grand Inquisitor.’ It’s a ridiculous piece of work, but I want to tell it to you.”
